section.title: The Call and Commission of Ezekiel
section.sectionRationale: The vision of chapter 1 now speaks. God stands Ezekiel on his feet, names him son of man, hands him a scroll of lamentation to eat, and sends him as a watchman to a rebellious house that may not listen. The call costs him bitterness, silence, and confinement before he ever preaches a word.
section.thesis: God commissions Ezekiel not by asking whether Israel will listen but by demanding faithfulness regardless of the response, feeding him His word before sending him to speak it, and making him a watchman whose warning, welcomed or refused, will always vindicate God's justice.
section.frameNote: Five scenes: standing him on his feet and naming the mission; the scroll of lamentation eaten and found sweet; sent to a hard-hearted people with a hardened face; the watchman's charge of life and death; and the glory that lifts him away, and the sign of silence.

units.label: Stood on his feet, sent to a rebellious house
units.note: ben-adam, son of man, named and commissioned

verses.text: “{{ben_adam|Son of man}}, ” He said to me, “stand up on your feet and I will speak to you.”
And as He spoke to me, the Spirit entered me and set me on my feet, and I heard Him speaking to me.
“Son of man,” He said to me, “I am sending you to the Israelites, to a rebellious nation that has rebelled against Me. To this very day they and their fathers have rebelled against Me.
They are obstinate and stubborn children. I am sending you to them, and you are to say to them, ‘This is what the Lord GOD says.’
And whether they listen or refuse to listen, for they are a rebellious house, they will know that a prophet has been among them.

But you, son of man, do not be afraid of them or their words. Do not be afraid, though briers and thorns surround you, and you dwell among scorpions. Do not be afraid of their words or dismayed by their presence, though they are a rebellious house.
But speak My words to them, whether they listen or refuse to listen, for they are rebellious.

units.label: The scroll eaten and found sweet
units.note: words of lamentation, sweet as honey

verses.text: And you, son of man, listen to what I tell you. Do not be rebellious like that rebellious house. Open your mouth and eat what I give you.”
Then I looked and saw a hand reaching out to me, and in it was a scroll,
which He unrolled before me. And written on the front and back of it were words of lamentation, mourning, and woe.
“Son of man,” He said to me, “eat what you find here. Eat this scroll, then go and speak to the house of Israel.”
So I opened my mouth, and He fed me the scroll.
“Son of man,” He said to me, “eat and fill your stomach with this scroll I am giving you.” So I ate, and it was as sweet as honey in my mouth.

units.label: Sent to a hard-hearted people
units.note: a forehead like flint against their hardness

verses.text: Then He said to me, “Son of man, go now to the house of Israel and speak My words to them.
For you are not being sent to a people of unfamiliar speech or difficult language, but to the house of Israel,
not to the many peoples of unfamiliar speech and difficult language whose words you cannot understand. Surely if I had sent you to them, they would have listened to you.
But the house of Israel will be unwilling to listen to you, since they are unwilling to listen to Me. For the whole house of Israel is hard-headed and hard-hearted.
Behold, I will make your face as hard as their faces, and your forehead as hard as their foreheads.
I will make your forehead like a diamond, harder than flint. Do not be afraid of them or dismayed at their presence, even though they are a rebellious house.”
“Son of man,” He added, “listen carefully to all the words I speak to you, and take them to heart.
Go to your people, the exiles; speak to them and tell them, ‘This is what the Lord GOD says,’ whether they listen or refuse to listen.”

units.label: The watchman's charge
units.note: blood on his hands, or not

verses.text: Then the Spirit lifted me up, and I heard a great rumbling sound behind me: ‘Blessed be the glory of the LORD in His dwelling place!’
It was the sound of the wings of the living creatures brushing against one another and the sound of the wheels beside them, a great rumbling sound.
So the Spirit lifted me up and took me away, and I went in bitterness and in the anger of my spirit, with the strong hand of the LORD upon me.
I came to the exiles at Tel-abib who dwelt by the River Kebar. And for seven days I sat where they sat and remained there among them, overwhelmed.
At the end of seven days the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, I have made you a {{tsofeh|watchman}} for the house of Israel. Whenever you hear a word from My mouth, give them a warning from Me.

If I say to the wicked man, ‘You will surely die,’ but you do not warn him or speak out to warn him from his wicked way to save his life, that wicked man will die in his iniquity, and I will hold you responsible for his blood.
But if you warn a wicked man and he does not turn from his wickedness and his wicked way, he will die in his iniquity, but you will have saved yourself.

Now if a righteous man turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity, and I put a stumbling block before him, he will die. If you did not warn him, he will die in his sin, and the righteous acts he did will not be remembered. And I will hold you responsible for his blood.
But if you warn the righteous man not to sin, and he does not sin, he will indeed live because he heeded your warning, and you will have saved yourself.”

units.label: The sign of silence
units.note: bound and made speechless until God opens his mouth

verses.text: And there the hand of the LORD was upon me, and He said to me, “Get up, go out to the plain, and there I will speak with you.”
So I got up and went out to the plain, and behold, the glory of the LORD was present there, like the glory I had seen by the River Kebar, and I fell facedown.
Then the Spirit entered me and set me on my feet. He spoke with me and said, “Go, shut yourself inside your house.
And you, son of man, they will tie with ropes, and you will be bound so that you cannot go out among the people.
I will make your tongue stick to the roof of your mouth, and you will be silent and unable to rebuke them, though they are a rebellious house.

But when I speak with you, I will open your mouth, and you are to tell them, ‘This is what the Lord GOD says.’ Whoever listens, let him listen; and whoever refuses, let him refuse, for they are a rebellious house.

ben_adam.gloss: Son of man, literally son of Adam, humanity itself. God addresses Ezekiel by this title more than ninety times in the book, stressing his frailty and creatureliness before the overwhelming glory just seen. Centuries later Jesus takes up this very title as His favorite self-designation, uniting true humanity with divine authority.

tsofeh.gloss: Watchman, one who keeps lookout on the walls to warn a city of approaching danger. God appoints Ezekiel a watchman for Israel: he does not control whether the people heed the warning, but he is answerable for whether he gives it.

basic.context: The vision that opened the book now becomes a voice. God stands the fallen prophet on his feet, calls him son of man, and sends him to a people who have rebelled against Him for generations. Before Ezekiel speaks a word to them, he must first eat: God hands him a scroll filled with lamentation, mourning, and woe, and, strangely, it tastes as sweet as honey. Then comes the hard commission, a rebellious house, a forehead made as hard as flint to match their hardness, and finally the sober charge of a watchman, responsible not for the outcome but for the warning.
basic.hermeneutics: This is Ezekiel's own call narrative, similar in shape to Isaiah 6 and Jeremiah 1, and it is meant to be read as real personal experience even as it uses vivid, symbolic actions, the eaten scroll, the hardened forehead, the bound tongue, to dramatize the prophet's task. The watchman image is a memorable illustration of responsibility, not a legal formula to be applied woodenly outside its pastoral point: faithfulness in delivering God's word, whatever the response.
basic.originalLanguages: God calls Ezekiel ben adam, son of man, a title of humble humanity rather than honor, used again and again to keep the prophet, and the reader, aware of the gap between the glory of chapter 1 and the frailty of the messenger. Later Ezekiel is made a tsofeh, a watchman, whose task is simply to sound the warning and leave the outcome to God and to the hearer.
basic.typology: Eating the scroll before speaking it foreshadows every true minister of God's word, who must first receive and digest it before proclaiming it, and points to Christ, the living Word, who perfectly embodied the message He preached. The watchman charge anticipates the New Testament's call to elders who must give an account for the souls entrusted to them.
basic.christ: Jesus took up the title Son of Man as His favorite self-description, filling it with far greater meaning than Ezekiel ever bore, both true humanity and, as Daniel 7 shows, everlasting divine authority. Where Ezekiel eats a scroll of lamentation, Jesus is Himself the Word made flesh, who bore in His own body the very sorrows His word announced, and who, unlike Ezekiel, was never silenced by unbelief but was raised to open every mouth that trusts Him.
basic.god: God is patient with human weakness, lifting Ezekiel to his feet again and again rather than despising his frailty, yet He is also unyielding about the mission: speak whether they listen or not. He holds His messenger to a standard of faithfulness in the warning, not success in the response, and He is just enough to hold every hearer responsible for their own iniquity.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 6:8-10 records a similar call amid a people who would not listen. Jeremiah 1:6-10 shows another reluctant prophet made bold by God's word in his mouth. Revelation 10:9-10 echoes Ezekiel's eaten scroll, sweet in the mouth yet bitter in effect.
basic.oneStory: This is the pattern for every true messenger of God across Scripture: chosen despite weakness, fed on God's word before speaking it, and sent to a world that may refuse to listen, all pointing to Jesus, the Son of Man and living Word, who both delivers and embodies the message that saves.

context.literary:
The section runs from 2:1 to 3:27 and is built as a series of speeches by God, each opening 'Son of man' and each followed by the prophet's compliance or silence. The movement is one of descent from vision to the street. The throne gives way to a voice, the voice commands an act of eating, the eating leads to a mission, the mission is interrupted by a journey, and the journey ends in a house where the prophet is shut up. The reader is carried from heaven's court to a quiet room in a village of exiles.

A pattern of repeated phrases ties the units together. The refrain 'whether they listen or refuse to listen' appears in 2:5, 2:7 and 3:11, and a related line closes the section at 3:27. 'Do not be afraid' is given three times in a single verse, 2:6. 'Rebellious house' is the section's signature, found in 2:5, 2:6, 2:7, 2:8, 3:9, 3:26 and 3:27. The repetition is a rhetorical drumbeat. It leaves the reader in no doubt about two things: the people will not hear, and God will not stop sending.

The structure also mirrors the classic prophetic call, with a divine encounter, a commission, an objection or fear to be overcome, and a sign. Where Isaiah's lips are cleansed and Jeremiah's mouth is touched, Ezekiel's mouth is filled. The scroll in 2:9-10 is written 'on the front and back', as the tablets were at Sinai, Exodus 32:15, a detail that implies a full text with nothing left to add. The section ends in a deliberate paradox: a prophet commissioned to speak is first made unable to speak, except when God opens his mouth, 3:27.
context.historical:
Ezekiel is sent to people who are not mere strangers but the nation's own leading families. The exiles of 597 BC were the elite, and they brought their expectations with them. They believed the temple would protect Jerusalem, and many assumed that the exile would be brief. In this setting a prophet announcing that the city would fall was telling the best-placed Judeans that their theology was wrong. The 'rebellious house' of 2:5 included men who would soon be sitting in Ezekiel's living room to ask for the word of the LORD, Ezekiel 8:1 and 14:1, and who would then ignore what they heard.

The charge of rebellion is old. God says the people and their fathers have rebelled 'to this very day', 2:3, and Ezekiel 20:8 traces the habit back to Egypt, before the exodus. The prophet is not telling the exiles something new about their character. He is naming a pattern that stretches across the nation's whole history.

The comparison in 3:5 to peoples of 'unfamiliar speech and difficult language' turns on the ancient assumption that a prophet had to share the language of his audience. Jesus makes a parallel argument when He says that Tyre and Sidon would have repented if they had seen the miracles done in Galilee, Matthew 11:21. Likewise, Nineveh listened to Jonah, Jonah 3:5, while Israel did not listen to its own prophets. The point is that the greater privilege carries the greater guilt.

The image of the watchman reflects the ordinary life of ancient cities. Watchmen stood on walls and towers to see danger early and to sound the horn, and the people were expected to heed it. Jeremiah 6:17 had used the figure of watchmen posted over Judah, and the people had answered, 'We will not listen!' By giving Ezekiel the title, God places him in the line of those whose task is to look and to speak, not to compel.
context.canonical:
This is one of the Bible's great call passages, and it stands in the company of Moses at the bush, Isaiah in the temple and Jeremiah in his youth. Jeremiah 1:6-10 is the closest parallel: a man who feels unfit is told not to be afraid, receives God's words in his mouth, and is set over nations. Ezekiel does not argue, as Moses and Jeremiah did, but his own mouth is filled and then closed. Isaiah 6:9-10 shows a similar commission to a people who will not understand, and Jesus and the apostles would use those words to explain Israel's resistance, Matthew 13:14-15 and John 12:37-41.

The eaten scroll has an Old Testament background of its own. Jeremiah says that when God's words were found, he ate them, and they were his joy, Jeremiah 15:16. Psalm 119:103 says God's words are sweeter than honey in the mouth, and Psalm 19:10 repeats the image. Deuteronomy 8:3 links God's words with the nourishment of life, which Jesus will quote when tempted, Matthew 4:4. Ezekiel's scroll joins these themes and adds the bitter content of lament and woe.

Revelation 10:9-10 picks up the scene directly. John is told to take a small scroll and eat it, and it is sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach, exactly the double experience of Ezekiel's commission, where the word is sweet to receive and bitter to carry, 3:14. The watchman of 3:17 returns in Ezekiel 33:7-9 where the charge is restated, and in the New Testament in Hebrews 13:17 and Acts 20:26-31. Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders, 'I am innocent of the blood of all men', Acts 20:26, is a conscious echo of 3:18-21. Finally, the title 'Son of Man', used about ninety times of Ezekiel, is taken from him and from Daniel 7:13 and given by Jesus to Himself.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The section is written to establish that Ezekiel's word has God's authority even when it is rejected. His first hearers needed to understand that the lack of a hearing does not undo the prophet's standing. The statement that 'they will know that a prophet has been among them', 2:5, promises that the word will be vindicated even if the people refuse it, and by the fall of Jerusalem it was. The author wants later readers to see that the failure of a message to persuade is not a sign that it was wrong.

He also wants to ground the prophet's confidence somewhere other than in himself. The Spirit sets Ezekiel on his feet, 2:2, God hardens his face, 3:8, and God fills his mouth, 3:2. Everything the prophet needs is given. The passage tells the exiles that the messenger is not a brave man who happens to have a message but a weak man whom God has made able. That is why the 'Son of man' title, with its emphasis on frailty, runs through the book.

The watchman charge speaks to Ezekiel and also to the exiles. They are told that each person is responsible for his own response, and that the prophet's warning is a gift to be taken seriously. Later chapters make this explicit, 18:23 and 33:11: God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but desires that they turn and live. The sober tone of 3:18-21 serves the purpose of that mercy, so that people will turn before it is too late.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The section describes events that belong to one man's call: the eaten scroll, the bound and silent prophet, the flint forehead. None of these is meant to be repeated. Christians are not asked to eat scrolls or accept physical muteness, and it would mistake the passage to build a technique of ministry from them. What is recorded is what God did to equip one prophet for one hard task.

What carries over is the pattern of the commission. The message comes from God before it comes from the messenger, and it must be received before it is spoken. Paul's charge to Timothy to 'preach the word', 2 Timothy 4:2, and his claim that he did not shrink from declaring the whole will of God, Acts 20:27, assume the same order. The assurance that faithfulness and not results measures the work also carries, for Jesus warned His disciples that they would be treated as He was, John 15:20.

The watchman principle must be handled with care. It is addressed to the prophet and tied to his office. The New Testament applies it to those who have charge of souls, Hebrews 13:17, and to every believer in the mutual care of Galatians 6:1 and James 5:19-20, but without turning each Christian into the guarantor of every neighbour's salvation. The passage does not say that unrepentant people perish because a messenger failed. It says the messenger who is silent is accountable for his silence, and the hearer who refuses is accountable for his refusal.

debates.question: Does the watchman principle in 3:17-21 describe a works-based salvation for the righteous man who turns to sin?

views.label: It addresses temporal or covenantal consequences, not final salvation
views.case: Ezekiel elsewhere insists the righteous will live and the wicked will die, language describing covenant life and death under Israel's national life, not a systematic statement on the eternal security of the individual believer.

views.label: It is a real moral warning about apostasy
views.case: Some read this alongside New Testament warnings to persevere, such as Hebrews 10:26-31, as showing that turning from righteousness to sin has real and serious consequences, whatever one's prior standing.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree the passage presses total seriousness about present obedience and warns against presuming on past righteousness; neither reading is meant to unsettle the finished, once-for-all salvation secured in Christ for those who trust Him.

debates.question: Was Ezekiel really struck dumb for years, 3:26-27?

views.label: A near complete muteness, broken only by oracles
views.case: The text says his tongue will cling to the roof of his mouth and that he will speak only when God opens his mouth. Ezekiel 24:27 and 33:21-22 describe the mouth being opened when news of the city's fall arrives, which suggests a long period of silence from 3:26 until then, with only prophetic speech between.

views.label: A restriction on one role only
views.case: The phrase is 'unable to rebuke', literally unable to be a man who reproves. On this view the prophet is cut off from the ordinary role of advocate and arbitrator among the exiles and so cannot argue with them, while still delivering God's word whenever commanded.

views.label: A symbolic frame for the book's arrangement
views.case: Some see the muteness as a literary or symbolic device marking off the oracles of judgment from the later oracles of hope, since the silence ends at 33:22 when the book turns to restoration.

debates.bearing: The grammar is compatible with each reading. In every case the lesson is the same: a prophet speaks only what God has said, and his silence is itself a sign to a people who will not hear.

debates.question: What does 'Son of man' mean when God says it to Ezekiel?

views.label: A reminder of human frailty
views.case: The Hebrew is ben adam, a son of Adam, as the BSB footnote notes. Used about ninety times, it marks the gap between the creature and the glory he has just seen, in the same sense as Psalm 8:4.

views.label: A prophetic title that points to Daniel's figure
views.case: The phrase gains weight once Daniel 7:13 uses it of one who receives everlasting dominion, and Jesus then makes it His chosen name. Ezekiel's use is closer to the first sense, but the later title builds on the same words.

debates.bearing: For Ezekiel the phrase is a humble title and no claim of dignity. Jesus takes the same words and fills them with a glory that the prophet only touched at the edges.

study.originalLanguages:
The address 'Son of man' is ben adam, literally 'son of Adam', which the BSB footnote notes with 'Or Son of Adam; here and throughout Ezekiel'. It is used of the prophet around ninety times. It is a title of humble creaturehood, set beside the glory of chapter 1. Psalm 8:4 uses the same pair of words to ask what a mere human is that God should care for him.

The people are called 'rebellious' repeatedly. The root is marad or meri, and the stock phrase bet meri, 'house of rebellion', occurs again and again in these chapters. It also appears as a noun, so that the people are not simply rebels but a house defined by rebellion. In 2:3 the word translated 'nation' is goy, a term usually used of the Gentile peoples, and the Hebrew puts it in the plural, so that Israel is described with the vocabulary of the nations it was meant to be distinct from.

Verse 4 calls the people 'obstinate and stubborn', literally hard of face and firm of heart. In 3:7 they are 'hard-headed', from the word for forehead, and 'hard-hearted'. God's answer in 3:8-9 turns on the same idea. He makes Ezekiel's face 'hard' to match theirs, using the root chazaq, 'to be strong', which is also the root of the prophet's name Yechezqel, 'God strengthens'. The forehead is made like shamir, translated 'diamond', a word that elsewhere names a hard stone used for engraving, as in Jeremiah 17:1, where Judah's sin is written with a diamond point on the tablet of the heart. A sin cut in the heart with a diamond is met by a prophet made as hard as the stone that cut it.

The scroll is a megillat sefer, a rolled book, and it is written 'front and back', as the tablets of the covenant were, Exodus 32:15. The contents are given as three words, a dirge, a moan and a cry of woe. The first is the plural of qinah, the funeral lament, and is the same family of word that gives the book of Lamentations its Hebrew alternative name. The prophet's first diet is grief.

Verse 3:3 has the instruction to eat, fill the belly and fill the stomach, and the scroll is as sweet as honey, from the word devash. Verse 3:14 records the other side of the experience: 'I went in bitterness and in the anger of my spirit', a bitterness that sits beside the sweetness and is not explained away.

In 3:15 the prophet sits among the exiles for seven days 'overwhelmed', from the root shamem, which means to be appalled or desolate. Seven days was the length of mourning in Job 2:13 and also the length of a priest's ordination, Leviticus 8:33, and for a priest-prophet the week may carry both senses.

The watchman is a tsofeh, from tsafah, to look out, and the verb for 'warn' is zahar. The Hebrew of 3:18 says that God will 'seek' the blood from the watchman's hand. Finally, the Spirit, ruach, 'entered' Ezekiel and set him on his feet in 2:2, in an act reminiscent of the breath that enters the bones in 37:10. In 3:12 the BSB footnote notes a textual difficulty, offering the alternative 'sound behind me as the glory of the LORD rose from its place', so the cry of blessing is itself uncertain.

typology.type: The scroll eaten, sweet and bitter, 2:8 to 3:3
typology.fulfillment: The prophet takes in God's word before he speaks it and finds it sweet to the taste and bitter to carry. Jesus lives in the same reality: He says man lives on every word from God's mouth, Matthew 4:4, and that the words He speaks are spirit and life, John 6:63. The correspondence deepens because the Word is a Person, John 1:1, who is the content and not only the carrier of the message, and who also bears its bitterness in the garden and at the cross. Revelation 10:9-10 uses Ezekiel's scene for the church's witness, sweet in the mouth and bitter in the stomach. The type falls short because Ezekiel digests a text, while the Son embodies the Word in His flesh.

God's repeated address marks Ezekiel as a frail representative among his people. Jesus takes the title and joins it to Daniel 7:13, where the Son of Man receives an everlasting dominion, Mark 14:62. He is also the Son of Man who has nowhere to lay His head, Matthew 8:20, who came to seek and to save the lost, Luke 19:10, and who came to give His life as a ransom, Mark 10:45. Ezekiel is only a representative of weakness, while Jesus enters the weakness in order to redeem it. The type falls short because the prophet is a man set against his people, and Christ is a man who stands in their place.

God hardens the prophet's face so that he will not be broken by those who are hard. Isaiah's Servant says 'I have set My face like flint', Isaiah 50:7, and Luke writes that Jesus 'resolutely set out for Jerusalem', Luke 9:51, with the language of a face set. The correspondence is of resolve in the face of opposition. The escalation is that Jesus walks toward the hostility not only to speak but to suffer under it. The type has limits in that Ezekiel's hardness was a protection given for his message, whereas Christ's steadfastness bore the weight of the people's rebellion on the cross.

The watchman who must warn of danger finds its fullest figure in the One Peter calls 'the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls', 1 Peter 2:25. Jesus wept over the city and told it what would bring peace, Luke 19:41-44, which is the watchman's cry spoken from within the city. He then delegated the task to elders who are to keep watch over the flock, Acts 20:28, and who will give account, Hebrews 13:17. The type falls short because Ezekiel could only warn, while Christ not only warns but lays down His life so the warned may live.

Ezekiel is silent except when God gives him words. Isaiah describes the Servant as one who 'did not open His mouth' before His accusers, Isaiah 53:7, and Matthew notes that Jesus gave no answer to any charge, Matthew 27:14. The parallel lies in silence under judgment. In Ezekiel the silence is a sign against a people who will not hear, and in Christ it is a willing submission to a sentence that was not His. The type falls short, because Jesus was not mute in His ministry but spoke with open mouth and authority, and the silence of the cross was an act and not a restriction.

study.christ:
The commission leads to Christ first by the title 'Son of man'. God uses it to Ezekiel about ninety times, and each time it reminds the prophet that he is dust beside the glory. In Daniel 7:13-14 the same words describe one who comes with the clouds and receives everlasting dominion, and Jesus put the two meanings together when He told the high priest that they would see the Son of Man 'sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven', Mark 14:62. He is the Son of Man who has no place to lay His head, Matthew 8:20, and the Son of Man who came to give His life as a ransom, Mark 10:45. Ezekiel's weakness and Daniel's glory belong together in Him.

It leads to Christ in the eating of the word. The prophet is fed the scroll before he is sent, and the one who lives by every word from the mouth of God, Matthew 4:4, is the one who can say His words are spirit and life, John 6:63. Jesus did not merely receive the word; He is the Word who was with God and was God, John 1:1. Where the prophet found the scroll sweet and then bitter, the Gospels show the Word made flesh tasting the full bitterness of the content, lament, mourning and woe, in the garden and on the cross. Revelation 5:1 then shows a scroll written on both sides in the hand of the One on the throne, and it is the Lamb who is found worthy to open it.

It leads to Christ in the commission to a people who will not listen. The reasons given in 3:5-7 are close to what Jesus said about Chorazin and Bethsaida, Matthew 11:21, and Stephen charged the leaders in Jerusalem with being stiff-necked, Acts 7:51. Jesus told His disciples that a servant is not above his master and that if they persecuted Him they would persecute them, John 15:20. The messenger is sent with the same promise of presence and the same expectation of refusal.

It leads to Christ in the watchman's care. The prophet is told to give a warning and is held to account for the blood of those he does not warn. Jesus is both the one who warns and the one who bears the consequence: He wept over Jerusalem and described what was coming, Luke 19:41-44, and went to the place of judgment Himself. Peter's phrase 'the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls', 1 Peter 2:25, gathers the figure.

It leads to Christ in the Spirit who stands the prophet on his feet. Ezekiel is raised when the Spirit enters him, 2:2, and the same Spirit later breathes life into the dry bones, 37:10. On the evening of the resurrection Jesus breathed on His disciples and said 'Receive the Holy Spirit', John 20:22, and the church is sent as the prophet was sent.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The scroll is not a cipher for a gospel text, and the watchman is not a disguised portrait of Jesus. The links stand where the New Testament itself uses these images, and they show how the prophet's weakness, his hunger for the word and his sending to rebels are made complete in Christ.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who speaks first. Before Ezekiel can answer, he is addressed, and before he can stand, he is told to stand. The initiative is God's from beginning to end, and the grace of the call is that it supplies what it demands. The command 'stand up on your feet' is followed in the next verse by the Spirit entering and setting him on his feet. The God who gives orders also gives the strength to obey, which is a pattern He keeps throughout Scripture.

He is honest about the task. He does not promise a response, and He says three times that the people may refuse. Many leaders would have spoken of a harvest. God speaks of rebellion and briers and scorpions, and then tells His prophet that he will not be afraid. The truthful framing is a kindness, because a man sent with false hopes would be crushed when they failed. God's candour about the hardness of the people is of a piece with His faithfulness in the preparation of the messenger.

He is patient with a rebellious people and does not give up on them. 'Whether they listen or refuse to listen' is not an indifference to the outcome. The very next verses, and the book's later chapters, say that He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and would rather they turn and live, Ezekiel 18:23 and 33:11. The watchman charge is a mercy, a warning given in advance to give people a chance to turn. He sends a prophet instead of striking, and keeps sending.

He is just in the allocation of responsibility. Each hearer is accountable for his own response, and each messenger is accountable for faithfulness in the delivery. 3:18-21 draws no line from the prophet's silence to the wicked man's guilt, since the man still dies in his iniquity, but it makes the silence a sin of its own. The measure of justice here is exact, with no blame carried by the wrong party.

He is present with the one He sends. The glory seen at the Kebar is seen again on the plain, 3:23, and the hand of the LORD is upon the prophet even when it is heavy, 3:14. The bitterness and anger of the prophet's spirit do not drive God away. For worship, the section teaches that we receive the word before we speak it, that we ask God for strength to match the work, and that He is faithful in the work He gives even when the response is silence.

crossReferences.note: Isaiah's call, with the same shape of an enthroned God sending a man to a people who will not understand. Both prophets are told the response will be refusal. Ezekiel's commission takes the pattern further by making the refusal part of the sign that a prophet has been among them.

Jeremiah protests he is only a child and is told not to be afraid, because God has put His words in his mouth. Ezekiel's mouth is filled by a scroll, not touched by a hand, but the message is the same: the prophet's equipment comes from God and the fear is overcome by presence.

Jeremiah says that God's words were found and he ate them, and they became his joy. It is the nearest prophetic parallel to the eaten scroll, and it shows that taking in the word is the way a prophet bears it, with joy and with sorrow together.

The psalmist says God's words are sweeter than honey in his mouth. The image explains why the scroll tastes like honey even though it is written with lament and woe, since the sweetness belongs to the truth of God's word and not to the pleasantness of its message.

John is told to eat a small scroll and it is sweet as honey in his mouth but bitter in his stomach. The New Testament uses Ezekiel's scene to describe the church's prophetic witness, which is sweet to receive and costly to deliver.

The watchman charge is repeated after the fall of Jerusalem, with the same terms of accountability. The repetition at the turning point of the book shows that what began as a call to one man is a standing principle of how God deals with those who warn and those who hear.

God asks whether He takes any pleasure in the death of the wicked and says He would prefer that they turn and live. This verse sets the severity of Ezekiel 3:18-21 inside the larger purpose of mercy, so that the watchman's warning is a means of life.

Paul tells the Ephesian elders that he is innocent of the blood of all, because he did not shrink from declaring the whole will of God. He applies the watchman principle to ministry in the new covenant, with the same weight of accountability.
Church leaders keep watch over souls as those who must give an account. The text carries the watchman's duty into the church and pairs it with a call to joyful cooperation by those who are led.

Jesus says Tyre and Sidon would have repented had they seen what Chorazin saw. This is the logic of Ezekiel 3:5-6: the greater the privilege the greater the guilt of refusing, and a prophet sent to those who share his language is not sent to the easy audience.

Jesus tells the high priest that the Son of Man will be seen at God's right hand and coming with the clouds. He draws together Ezekiel's humble title with Daniel's vision of dominion, and in doing so takes the name God gave Ezekiel into the heart of His own claim.

The Servant sets His face like flint, knowing He will not be put to shame. The image echoes the forehead made like a diamond in Ezekiel 3:9, and the New Testament sees in the Servant's resolve the pattern for Jesus' own journey to Jerusalem.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning, God has spoken and people have been called to hear. In Genesis 3, the first question is 'Where are you?', and the story from there is a long record of God sending messengers to a people who hide. Moses is sent, then prophet after prophet, each standing between a holy God and a hard-hearted people. Ezekiel's call sits at the moment when that history looks most discouraged. The temple is about to fall, the exiles are listening to false hope, and God sends one more messenger with the clearest warning yet.

The call also adds something new. Ezekiel is a priest sent as a prophet, a man who could have offered sacrifices and is instead given a word. He is the 'Son of man' sent to his own people, and he is filled with God's words and the Spirit. The scroll and the Spirit are what the prophets before him lacked in vivid form, and they point toward the promise that God's word and Spirit will be placed inside His people, Ezekiel 36:26-27 and Jeremiah 31:33. The prophet carries a hint of the new covenant in his own body.

The watchman charge sets up the book's main argument. Chapter 18 will insist that each person answers for his own life and that God desires repentance, and chapter 33 will repeat the charge as the city falls. The story's next turning point is the one the people denied: Jerusalem's ruin, followed by the promise of a new heart, dry bones breathing and a temple filled again.

In Christ the call finds its fullest answer. He is the Son of Man who warns, who weeps over Jerusalem, who is sent to a house that will not listen, and who is faithful to the end. He is the Word that was eaten and lived by, and the Shepherd and Overseer of souls. His Spirit is given to those who trust Him, and they are sent in turn, as in Acts 1:8, to a world that may refuse.

The story ends with a scroll that no prophet could open. Revelation 5 shows it in the hand of the One on the throne, and the Lamb is found worthy to open it. The long line of messengers ends in a place where no one needs to be warned, because those who dwell there will see His face, Revelation 22:4, and the word that was bitter in the belly is only sweetness.

sermon.title: The Call of a Prophet in Declining Times (Part 1)
sermon.why: Carson preaches through Ezekiel 1 to 3 together, tracing how the vision of glory in chapter 1 becomes the call and commission of chapters 2 and 3, and drawing out what it means to be faithful in declining, resistant times.

quiz.q: What title does God repeatedly use to address Ezekiel in this commission?

options.text: Priest of the Most High.
options.note: He is a priest by training, but that is not the title used here.

options.text: Son of man, stressing his humble humanity before God's glory.
options.note: The title ben adam recurs throughout the call narrative.

options.text: Servant of the covenant.
options.note: This is not the title used in the commission.

options.text: Watchman of Israel, used from the very first verse.
options.note: Watchman comes later in 3:17; the opening address is son of man.

quiz.q: What was written on the scroll God gave Ezekiel to eat?

options.text: Blessings and promises of prosperity.
options.note: The content is lament and woe, not blessing.

options.text: Nothing; the scroll was blank.
options.note: It was written on the front and the back.

options.text: Words of lamentation, mourning, and woe.
options.note: Ezekiel 2:10 describes the scroll's contents exactly this way.

options.text: A list of Israel's future kings.
options.note: The scroll contains sorrowful judgment, not a king list.

quiz.q: How did the scroll taste when Ezekiel ate it?

options.text: He refused to eat it.
options.note: He eats it as commanded and describes its sweetness.

options.text: Bitter and unbearable.
options.note: The taste is described as sweet, not bitter.

options.text: Like ordinary bread.
options.note: The text specifies honey-like sweetness, a striking detail.

options.text: As sweet as honey, despite its message of woe.
options.note: Ezekiel 3:3 records this surprising sweetness.

quiz.q: According to the watchman charge, what is Ezekiel responsible for?

options.text: Faithfully giving the warning, not controlling whether people respond.
options.note: Ezekiel 3:18-21 ties his responsibility to whether he warns, not to the outcome.

options.text: Punishing the wicked himself.
options.note: Punishment belongs to God; Ezekiel's task is to warn.

options.text: Guaranteeing that everyone he warns repents.
options.note: He cannot guarantee repentance; he is responsible only to warn.

options.text: Nothing; the passage assigns no responsibility to him.
options.note: The whole passage is built around his solemn responsibility to warn.

quiz.q: What happened to Ezekiel's speech at the end of chapter 3?

options.text: He was given unlimited freedom to speak whenever he wished.
options.note: The opposite occurs; his speech is restricted by God.

options.text: He lost his voice permanently with no hope of restoration.
options.note: God promises to open his mouth again when He speaks with him.

options.text: God made him silent and bound, his tongue stuck to the roof of his mouth, until God chose to open it.
options.note: Ezekiel 3:24-27 describes this sign of enforced silence.

options.text: Nothing changed about his speech.
options.note: A clear and deliberate sign of silence is imposed.

questions: Ezekiel had to eat the scroll, receiving God's word into himself, before he could speak it to others. Where in your life do you need to let Scripture shape you more deeply before you try to speak it to someone else?
The scroll was full of lamentation and woe, yet tasted sweet as honey. Have you experienced God's hard truths as, in the end, sweet and good for you? What made the difference?
The watchman is responsible for the warning, not for whether it is heeded. Where do you carry guilt or pressure for someone else's response that is not actually yours to bear?
Ezekiel sat overwhelmed among the exiles for seven days before he spoke a word. How comfortable are you sitting in silence and grief with people before rushing to give them answers?

God made Ezekiel's face as hard as flint to match a hard-hearted people, yet also fed him with sweetness first. How do steadfastness and tenderness need to work together in your own callings this week?

translationNotes.note: Son of man is a plain, humble title, son of Adam, emphasizing Ezekiel's humanity rather than any special honor; it stands in stark contrast to the glory just described in chapter 1.

In bitterness and in the anger of my spirit can describe either Ezekiel's own emotional turmoil at his commission or a bitterness shared with, or given by, the Spirit; translators differ on whose bitterness is meant.

The tongue sticking to the roof of the mouth pictures an imposed, sign-act muteness; Ezekiel is not mute in every sense but is restricted from freely rebuking the people until God gives him a specific word to speak.
